We understand that the regulations are not ready and they cannot be intelligently debated until they are. The committee ought to rise and report progress, and the house should be moved into supply so that the Senn amendment may be proceeded with.

According to the statement made by the minister, it does not make any difference whether 10 acres or 100 acres are under cultivation on the quarters on which the mortgage is placed; the man who holds the mortgage still receives one-third of the benefit. In my opinion the man who holds the mortgage is entitled to one-third on the quarter on which he holds the mortgage only.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The reason for that provision is that it is quite possible for the reverse to be the case; that is for all the wheat to be on the land in which the mortgagee has an interest and none on the land in which the renter has an interest, or that the owner who has a mortgage on has an interest in. If this provision were not in, the mortgagee would draw one-third on all the reduction in the wheat acreage; but as it is now, if the mortgage was all on a quarter, then he would only draw one-third of one-third in the case of a three-quarter section farm. It makes it much better for the renter or owner.

There is one point I should like the minister to clear up. I referred to it yesterday, as did also the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw). Summer-fallow has to be completed by August 1, but the bonus can be paid after July 1. If a man receives the bonus, say on July 7 or July 14, is there anything to prevent him from sowing that land to green feed? That is considered a sound practice in many parts.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is nothing to prevent him from doing it, but if he does so, it may result in the treasury, which after all pays the amounts, asking him to wait until it is absolutely certain that he has not cut it for grain before he can draw any payment on the summer-fallow. I would imagine what would happen would be that immediately it is sown, the payments would be held up until the farmer could prove that he had not cut this crop for grain.
It would be all right to cut it for green feed?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I would think so, but I should not like to be too definite at the moment, because these regulations are not

interpreted by me when it comes to making payment; they are interpreted by the organization which checks payments.
If he cuts the crop when green, before it is sufficiently matured to thresh, that should be sufficient proof that he is not going to thresh it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is pretty much the same as the rye, which might be handled in the same way, and they might refuse to make the final payment until later. I should not like to make an interpretation at the moment.

I would be the last one in the house to try to hold up any of these proceedings; I am as anxious as anyone to help the minister to evolve something which would help the farmers of western Canada, but from what I have seen the last day or two, certainly there is confusion. I do not think there is any hon. member who understands these regulations now. We have an order in council dated April 2, and I presume there will have to be another to embody these other regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They are all passed.

Briefly I want to protest against this whole proceeding. This house has been in session for over seven weeks, and we should have had this long ago. It is the same thing as the minister tried to put over last July 25. He wanted to have a bill proceeded with that was not even printed; other hon. members and myself protested, and we had to make an agreement then that the bill would be proceeded with and the general discussion take place afterward. We had not seen the bill at all. The same thing is happening to-day. We cannot intelligently discuss this matter as it stands; the committee might just as well rise and let the other discussion go on.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The committee had all the regulations before them to discuss, had them presented here and discussed very fully yesterday evening. The committee now have before them all the changes; not in printed form, but they have been read in exactly the same way as the amendment to any bill is always read to this committee when changes are made. Whenever there are amendments they are simply read to the committee and the committee accepts or rejects them. They have been read this afternoon, but in addition I have asked the staff in the office to prepare as quickly as possible mimeographed copies of the whole regulations as now drafted and passed, and they should be here at any time. If it is desired by the committee-but I understand it is not-that the discussion should

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
continue on these particular regulations or on the general policy itself, after all it is the vote that is under consideration, not these regulations particularly. The matter under consideration at the moment is the question whether we shall vote $35,000,000 for this purpose. The only thing we are going to do if we delay that is to prevent the payment of any money until at least some weeks after we come back here following the Easter recess. It will have no other effect.

If we do pass the estimate to-night the minister cannot spend any of that money, because a bill has to be based on the estimate. It must go through its readings here, go to the senate and receive the royal assent. That cannot possibly be done before May 15. So the minister's reasoning is wiped off the slate.
As to the illustration the minister gave with respect to amendments to bills passing through the house, I suggest that is hardly comparable with this. Here we have a new set of regulations. How can hon. members follow these things, no matter how elaborate the explanation the minister gives? To-day I attempted to follow a statement made by the Minister of Finance with respect to the excess profits tax proposals that will be included in the budget. Hon. gentlemen here gave close attention to those proposals; I wonder how many of them could state right now what the Minister of Finance was proposing. I have in mind three or four out of the dozen or so; they stick in my mind possibly because I approved them.
The minister does not need this money now; he cannot spend it legally until he gets this estimate through. I dare say he will want money for administration. He will have to secure that in the extraordinary manner that the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act provides, and I have no doubt he will get it, since in days gone by he has not been backward in asking for governor general's warrants.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
One would, of course,
feel much more free in proceeding with the matter if the money were passed by the house before the recess. When we come back we shall have to go through the form of passing it, and some time may be taken in doing so, which may delay us considerably in getting on with the payments for administration. But the matter which is of much greater importance is emphasized by what has just been said. When a minister rises in his place and reads something to the house or the committee, it is impossible for hon. members listening to get the whole meaning of it. If, however, he were permitted to discuss it for an hour after it had been read,
I think we would all go away with a definite idea of what it means. The very remark made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is, I suggest, an important reason why that would be a good thing to do. He says he is going away from here confused as to what this means. As soon as this house adjourns I intend to leave for my constituency to see that the people there are not confused about what it means, and I presume every other hon. member would like to do the same thing. I would hope that every hon. member, on both sides of the house, whether he believes in it or not, will at least make known to the farmers the possibilities under it; and if an hour or an hour and a half could be spent in clearing up some of the confusion in the mind of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, I think it would be time well spent.

Not only in my mind;
I think in the minds of the 245 members.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I will not admit that
I am among that number, though that may be because I have had to direct the drafting of the regulations. The question is simply whether we wish to have full knowledge of what the regulations mean. I might suggest also that it will not make a great deal of difference, because, after all, I suppose we shall have to proceed with the debate on the amendment.

I do not like this whole policy; but I think if, before this house adjourns for the Easter recess, we can have a discussion of the regulations as amended, in order to understand them thoroughly, we shall be in a much better position to inform our constituents with regard to the policy. I should like very much to see the regulations, which now are being mimeographed, brought down and discussed. As I say, I do not like the policy; I think it is going to be very difficult to work out, and I do not believe it will assist the small farmer to the extent I had hoped. I am not going to discuss that phase of the question just now; but in spite of the fact that I do not care for the suggestions that have been made, still I think it would be in the interests of all if we could understand them. Then we would make no mistake in anything we said about them.

When we get back to our constituencies the farmers will be starting their seeding operations, and they will want to know exactly what is the policy of the government with regard to wheat. I should like to know whether the policy described by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is law. If so, I should like to know how it became law, whether it was passed by order



Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
in council. We have not had anything of that kind put through this house as yet. Can we assure the farmers that they will be paid on a quota based on sixty-five per cent of last year's wheat acreage? Is that definite, or is it just something the minister thinks may be put into effect? We have had published in the press already the regulations drawn up by the Minister of Agriculture, and the people of the west have been told that those are the regulations under which they are going to operate. But already those regulations have been amended to a considerable extent. Have we any assurance now that the policy set out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to continue to be the policy, or will that be amended also? The farmers should know definitely and at once what is to be the policy of this government. Seeding is already starting, and it is not fair to the farmers to expect them to conduct their operations in such a way as to comply with regulations which may not be the policy a short time from now. We should have something definite before we leave this house.
So far as my statement is concerned, the policy outlined is that of this government.
Has it been passed yet?
Yes.
By order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. The wheat board act provides for an initial payment of 70 cents and for participation certificates. It also provides for the setting up of a quota; the wheat board is given power to do that. There is no legislation required; that is a matter of policy which was decided last year. As I understand it, every organization interested has passed resolutions asking that the quota system be continued this year.

Is there anything to prevent the wheat board from changing that policy between now and harvest time, to say that they will accept on a basis of only forty per cent of last year's acreage, we will say? Is there anything to prevent that being done, or is the minister just telling parliament that this will likely be the policy? What assurance have we that this will be followed out? We have had many changes in the last few years, many amendments and many regulations. For instance, we had the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which was passed by this house; then regulations were introduced which largely destroyed the principle of certain parts of that act. I do not think this situation is at all satisfactory.

Perhaps we could save a little time in this discussion. As I said the other day, I am very much opposed to the manner in which this question is being handled, but I quite agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that we should be able to discuss this question with our people as intelligently as possible. We cannot discuss this matter intelligently without having the amended regulations before us, but those we have not got and cannot get. Could we not adjourn this discussion, continue the debate on the amendment, and then later come back to these regulations when we can discuss them more intelligently? I certainly think we should try to take home to our people as much information as possible.

Speaking on March 12, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
To accomplish this a definite limit will be set on the amount of wheat which it will be possible to deliver either to the board, on the open market or otherwise, during the crop year 1941-42. The limit will be 230 million bushels -for the whole of Canada, an amount which it hopes can be sold in the domestic and export markets in 1941-42.
Is that amount definite? Have we legislation to the effect that not more than 230 million bushels can be sold, to the board or otherwise, during the course of the year? Or is there a possibility that this figure may be changed?
Mr. MacKINNON (Edmonton West)-: The amount set out, 230 million bushels, is the figure beyond which we do not propose to take wheat from the farmers of Canada.
That is definite, is it?
That is definite.

I should like to read a statement which shows the confusion existing at the present time with regard to the policy enunciated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have before me a copy of an analysis sent out by the board of trade of Calgary, which states:
The policy in brief.
The wheat board to be authorized to accept from producers in all Canada, 230,000,009 bushels at a price of 70 cents basis No. 1 northern, Fort William.
Deliveries to be accepted from each individual producer on the basis of 65 per cent of last Shear's sworn acreage.
A general quota of 5 bushels per acre to apply to first deliveries.
That is the point that causes confusion:
Balance of total to be taken on_ a pro rata basis, based on average yield in 1941 at shipping points, as per schedule below:

I notice that the publication issued by the wheat pool gives the same table. This has been sent throughout the country as the quota for this year. Can the Minister of Trade
and Commerce assure us that this will be the quota?

I have seen the statement to which the hon. member refers; as a matter of fact, a copy was sent to me by the Calgary board of trade. I did not go into it very thoroughly, but I did read it, and I can say that the figure quoted with regard to the average yield of twenty-five bushels is correct. I have not compared that figure with other suggested or possible yields, but as I have already stated there will be a five-bushel general quota, and the succeeding quotas will be based on the yield at the shipping point, on 65 per cent of the wheat acreage of 1940.

The minister states that
19-54 bushels will be accepted on a 25-bushel . yield. I do not think that is correct. Supposing this year we had an average yield of twenty-five bushels to the acre. Can the minister say that the board would allow everyone to deliver 19-54 bushels on 65 per cent of last year's acreage, and pay the initial payment? They could not begin to do it, so that figure is not correct. It shows the confusion that exists. I do not know who is responsible for this thing being sent out-they are being 'sent to other countries, I believe. The Alberta wheat pool forwarded them, and I say there should be a statement by the government pointing out what the government's policy really is. At the present time no policy has been stated. The minister could not tell me what it is.

No one can say at this time what the quota is going to be. That cannot be stated until we see what the crop is. It may be that we will be able to accept, in the amount of
230,000,000 bushels, all of the wheat grown in western Canada this year. But we will not know that until we understand the nature of the crop. We will not know it until we have an opportunity to survey the diversification of the yield in western Canada. We will not be able to state the quota until the crop is well under way.

Will it not be possible for the wheat board, the government, or the Department of Trade and Commerce to issue a statement to the press pointing out that there is no authority for the statement to which I have referred? Otherwise the farmers will be badly fooled in their operations.
Neither my department nor any department of government so far as I know is responsible for the statement to which the hon. member refers.
Where did it come from?

I have no idea where it came from. As a matter of fact I am going on the air to-night to make a preliminary statement on wheat. I believe the Minister of Agriculture is going to use the radio, and from time to time the wheat board will be using it, to make statements concerning regulations.
Will the open trade be in a position to take wheat? Is there anything in the act to prevent that?

There are two matters connected with this problem to which I suggest the minister should give attention. The first is the reduction of acreage. If I understand correctly the proportion which
230.000.	000 bears to the crop in 1940, should the crop in 1941 be equal to that of 1940 it would mean that 46 per cent of the acreage now in crop would produce the amount of
230.000.	000 bushels. The result would be that the western farmer will have on hand many millions of bushels which would be unsaleable.
The other point is that the government has seen fit to continue the initial price of 70 cents a bushel. I think the committee has a right to know why 70 cents is going to be the rate per bushel this year, the same as it was last year. Having regard to the fact that the farmer will find himself on a reduced standard of living, in consequence of reductions he must necessarily effect, under the reduction of his saleable crop of wheat, why is it the House of Commons has not been informed as to the price being received by the wheat board from the United Kingdom? When the question was asked last session I believe it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce who said he could not give an answer because it would not be in the public interest so to do.
There has been a debate in the Saskatchewan legislature in the last few weeks, particularly on the last day of February, on

the subject of wheat. During that debate speeches were made by the premier of Saskatchewan and the provincial minister of agriculture. Certain recommendations were made by the legislature which have already been placed before this committee. I shall not go into detail respecting those recommendations, except to say that the first was that the minimum price for the 1941 wheat crop should be set at 85 cents a bushel basis No. 1 Fort William. The reason for the recommendation by that legislature-one which was unanimously adopted-calling upon the government of Canada to fix the price at 85 cents was that when the matter was before the legislature it was within the contemplation both of the premier and of the minister of agriculture of the province that there would be a reduction this year to 230,000,000 bushels.
Time and again we have asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce the price the Canadian government is receiving from the government of the United Kingdom. Hon. members have not been able to get that information. Yet they have the information in the legislature of Saskatchewan. The premier is reported to have said that-and I quote from the Canadian Press report:
The suggested price of 85 cents a bushel would not be acceptable to all-
He went on to point out that it would be impossible for farmers, even on that basis, to pay their debts.
-but it was an increase over the present price of 70 cents. The reason this figure was suggested was that it was the price which Great Britain was prepared to pay. It was reasonable and fair and would not be a burden upon the mother country.
I am asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce if the premier of Saskatchewan was justified in making that statement. Did he have any information which was not available to members of the House of Commons?
I turn now to the remarks of the minister of agriculture in the legislature of Saskatchewan. He would be in a particularly good position to say what the United Kingdom is paying for wheat, because, if I remember correctly, he accompanied the federal Minister of Agriculture to the old country. This is the press report concerning his comments: An objection that the price-
That is, 85 cents a bushel.
-was too high was not valid because Great Britain was already paying that figure for Canadian wheat now and was willing to continue paying it. Canada therefore would not be imposing on Great Britain.
Surely the minister could inform the committee what Canada is receiving, so that we may be in a position to know whether we 
would be justified in supporting the resolution now before the committee, and whether there is any justification for setting the price at 70 cents.
Speaking during the last campaign in western Canada the Minister of Agriculture made the statement on numerous occasions that the British government was paying sufficient to enable a further interim payment of from 10 to 12 cents per bushel. In other words, the British government was paying from 82 to 85 cents a bushel. That is the necessary inference from the statement. Surely this committee has the right to know now something which apparently is known to the premier of Saskatchewan and the minister of agriculture in that legislature.
Mr. Chairman, I cannot say where the premier of Saskatchewan or the minister of agriculture in that province got the figures to which the hon. member has referred-
Are they not correct?
but I can say they are not correct.
Are they very far out?

The Minister has not given a satisfactory answer to the questions which have been asked. When the Minister of Agriculture introduced the vote on March 27 he placed on record representations made by the advisory committee of the wheat board and the Federation of Agriculture. Later I placed on record representations made by the Saskatchewan legislature. There has been no reference by the minister to anything of importance in those representations. I may add that the resolution passed in the Saskatchewan legislature had been accepted by the wheat pools and endorsed by the United Farmers of Saskatchewan.
All those representations referred to increased prices. In fact the resolution passed by the Saskatchewan legislature went so far as to suggest an initial price of 85 cents. Nothing has been placed before the committee giving any reason for the government's statement that it intends to leave the initial price at 70 cents. The impression has gone out among those in wheat circles that the price paid by the British government for the last consignment of wheat which the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced in the house last summer was close to 85 cents. I have heard the exact figure, but whether or not it is correct I am not prepared to put it on Hansard. My information is that it is slightly more than 85 cents. Now when the British

Supply-Agriculture

Wheat Acreages
government paid a price in that neighbourhood for our wheat, and when the wheat board gets a fifteen cent processing levy on every bushel of wheat milled for domestic consumption, and in view further of the fact that the government is going to take delivery of
230,000,000 bushels of wheat this year which will cover only the wheat sold to Great Britain and the wheat used for domestic consumption, this house should have a statement from the minister that it is not possible to pay an initial price of 85 cents without constituting a drain upon the treasury. Certainly the minister should state why the price should continue at 70 cents when the committee has good reason to believe that the wheat is being sold to Great Britain for more than 70 cents, and the wheat sold for domestic consumption is bringing in more than 70 cents. We should know why the wheat board proposes to leave the initial price this year at a figure which the government admitted last year was far below the cost of production to the wheat grower.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think any member of this house from western Canada would deny that the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Mines and Resources and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as three members of the wheat subcommittee of the cabinet, would be very anxious to increase the price upwards from 70 cents if the figure suggested now by the hon. member was what was received for our wheat. On that particular point, and speaking personally, I am not just sure that the same reason for secrecy prevails at the moment as it did when I made the statement last July that it was not in the public interest to give the exact figure for which the wheat was sold to the British government. Nevertheless I am not in a position to give that now. I should first want to consult our advisers, the wheat board, on whose advice largely we decided last year that it was not in the public interest to give the exact figures paid by the British government for the wheat we sold last year.

It will
make it bad for you if you are getting more than that and the farmers are not getting a fair deal.
I was interested in the minister's explanation. May I ask what the difference was between-
I do not propose to allow myself to be drawn into making a statement of that kind. I want to make very sure of what the position is before I give any figures.

The reason I ask is this. In the monthly bulletin of agricultural statistics issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, at page 387, is set out the number of bushels of wheat that were shipped via the Canadian Atlantic seaboard to the United Kingdom in the four months ending November 1939 and for the same four months in 1940. The quantity shipped in the four months ending November 1939 was 14,747,148 bushels, and the amount paid by the United Kingdom was $10,194,765. During the same four months in 1940 the amount shipped by way of Atlantic ports to the United Kingdom was 23,984,555 bushels, approximately 24,000,000 bushels, for which the Canadian government received $21,630,721. Apparently therefore in the records of the minister's own department there is some indication of the price that was paid, which is well in advance of 80 cents, as a simple calculation will show. Are these the prices received by the Canadian government or by the wheat board f.o.b. an eastern port, or are they the prices received in the old country out of which freight has to be paid?
It is not possible for me to give that information offhand. I am not sure whether the context from which my hon. friend is reading shows it or not, but if not I would have to make inquiries.

I am reading
from the monthly bulletin issued by the minister himself for December, 1940.
There is no doubt that any document issued by the bureau referred to would be accurate, but whether that bears out the contention as to the price per bushel is a different matter.

What I am trying to get at is this. The statistics are available here. They have not been given to the house on the ground of public interest, but we can arrive at our own conclusion if the minister will state whether this is the net price received or the price out of which freight has to be paid.
I cannot give that information now.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
If I might be permitted the newspaper report answered my hon. friend's question because it said there was a $6,000,000 loss. That was put out by the same authority which published the document from which my hon. friend is taking his

figures. It was put out three or four weeks ago, showing a loss of $6,000,000 on the 1939 crop.
The Minister of Agriculture must be astray; either that or he was not paying attention. I am reading from the monthly bulletin issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Every week or every few weeks that same authority puts out a statement in the press, and it will be recalled that a very few weeks ago the statement was put out that there was a $6,000,000 loss on the 1939 crop. That $6,000,000 loss indicated that there must have been, between the 70 cents paid on the farmer's wheat and the price received from the British government, sufficient by way of costs to wipe out the entire difference and create over and above that a loss of $6,000,000.

I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce for an answer to my question so that the committee would know exactly what price was being received. So far as the explanation of the Minister of Agriculture is concerned, that because there was a loss of $6,000,000, the wheat board did not secure a high enough price from the United Kingdom, let me point out that that was not the stand he took some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not saying that they did not secure a high enough price from the United Kingdom. I say that the 70 cent advance paid to the farmer was sufficient to result in a $6,000,000 loss on the part of the 1939 crop sold, after you take the costs out of the price which the British government and others paid. I am not saying that the British government did not pay enough.

On this wheat
there was a loss of $6,000,000, according to the Minister of Agriculture, and it could have been sold last February and March by the wheat board, not at a loss, but at such a price that there would have been available to the farmers an additional 10 to 12 cents a bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It could not.
I will read what the Minister of Agriculture said.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I know what you are going to read. You have read it often. I know what it says and what it means.

The people of
western Canada, having listened to what the Minister of Agriculture said, unfortunately put

a different interpretation upon his words than he meant to convey, if he meant to convey what he says to-day. This is what he said:
The Canadian government can sell to Britain,.-
I am referring now to the report of a speech made on March 6, 1940.
-through the wheat board, all the wheat they now have on hand, and thereby pay those who sold to the board an additional 10 or 12 cents per bushel, stated the Hon. James G. Gardiner, dominion Minister of Agriculture. . . .
Mr. Gardiner said that if the wheat were sold now, Britain would pay the storage until they actually took delivery, instead of the farmers who will pay the storage until it is sold.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: "If it were sold now."
If the wheat were sold now.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: And I might tell my hon. friend that the last time he read that document in -his own constituency, one of the men who was listening to him got up and gave the audience his interpretation of what I gave in the same hall, and it was what I gave.
That is perfectly true. But let me go on.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In other words, I did not give a wrong interpretation.

Mr. Chairman, if
the hon. gentleman will just wait, possibly the last words will clear up the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: But you are reading from a newspaper report.

The newspaper
report, now, is not correct?
It was not correct then.

In spite of this fact, Mr. Gardiner said, my government believes that it is better business for the farmers not to sell at the present price.
What possible meaning would there be in that, Mr. Chairman, other than this, that the government-

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The meaning was that
we did not know at the time that France was going to fall.
The answer now is that they did not know at the time that France was going to fall. The only difference which the fall of France made to the situation-

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Was a hundred million bushels of wheat.

Was fifty millions, including the Netherlands, France and Belgium.

a war.

Fifty million bushels. Now I again ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce this question, why should the committee and the house not have this information? Are the farmers not interested? Is it not their wheat that is being dealt with? Have they not the right to know what is being received, what the proceeds are, when they are being asked to produce wheat during a time of war at a loss, in many cases-the only industry operating under that disadvantage? Have not they, being asked to do a patriotic duty-the one industry in Canada required to produce at a loss-the right to know what is being received for the product they produce?
Mr. Chairman, I would not for anything attempt to interfere with my hon. friend making a speech, but I have already given him the answer to the question which he has just asked.

Not a very

The answer is that I am not in a position to reveal the information asked for by the hon. member at this time.

I should like to ask the

Then, next day, speaking in favour of the processing tax, he made this statement: that they were charging Britain more than they were charging the people of Canada, therefore the Canadian people ought to be prepared to pay the 15 cents processing tax. What did he mean by that-that they were charging Britain more than they were charging the people of Canada?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The question
is irrelevant because it refers to another debate in this session.

That was not this session.
It was last session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Oh, that is different.

Let us have an answer to
that.
Well, I am not prepared just at the moment to give an answer.

That reply makes it all
the more evident that we should have a thorough investigation into this whole matter. The minister does not know anything about his department. I venture to say that he does not know to-day how much cash wheat they have, what options they are. selling, where their cash wheat is, what they have sold, and what they have sold it at. We should have a report on this whole matter. It is tied in with this other scheme, and we do not know the facts, and the minister doesn't know.
He knows quite a bit about it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
One or two matters have been brought up in the discussion, which, I think, require a statement in view of the fact that they bear upon both the policy announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the policy which I announced the other day.
I have before me Hansard of November 14, 1940, and April 4, 1941. The latter contains three or four speeches which were delivered1 in committee on the estimate now under consideration, and in those speeches certain references were made to matters which have been under discussion during the last few moments. In these speeches, too, the speakers referred to addresses which they had made on previous occasions. I have here the address which was made by the hon. member for Souris, to which he referred, on November 14, and in which he made the statement that last year he had proposed a scheme very similar to the one which is now before the committee. But he did not enlarge upon it or indicate what he said to the house on that occasion, and I should like to put it on Hansard.
It is out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is not out of order. That was last session.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; you have just finished ruling one hon. member out of order for quoting or asking about something that had been debated at this session. I would remind you that November 14 was this session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I should like to point out that it is always advisable and necessary, when an hon. members reads from a statement, that he indicate what he is reading from; it is helpful in determining a point of order.

I have no objection to the minister quoting from what I said. I merely thought that we should be consistent in the matter of procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

Go ahead.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I quote:
I am going to suggest to the government also that earnest thought be given to a plan which might have a far-reaching effect. For some years I have thought that we must work out a soil conservation programme in western Canada. This has been done with success in other countries. I know some will object to the cost involved in any such programme, but let me state in general terms what I have in mind. Supposing you took the total cultivated area of the prairies and paid the producers $5 an acre for summer-fallowing one-third of that area.
That, I submit, is almost exactly what we are proposing here. The only difference is that this is $5 instead of $4.
What is the total cultivated acreage?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We are attempting to reduce the total cultivated acreage by 35 per cent, approximately one-third, by paying $4 an acre.
Excuse me; that is the total cultivated acreage of all crops? This is wheat acreage.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
About 43 million acres is the total. He goes on:
That may seem to involve a tremendous amount of money, but I suggest that the cost would not be any greater than the amount paid under the acreage bonus and the guaranteed price, and certainly there would be a great improvement in farming methods.
[The Chairman.]
In the same speech my hon. friend went on to discuss matters of more grass, coarse grains, and so on. I am sure he will agree that the present policy is the proper one to bring before the house at this time, particularly in view of the fact that he himself has made a success of farming in that section of Manitoba where that kind of farming is absolutely essential. I would say the same with regard to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). In a speech the other night he referred to an address he made in November of last year and also to the fact that he farms now very much in the manner we are suggesting that others should farm through the policy now before the house. I could understand either hon. gentleman objecting to payments by way of bonus being made to other persons in view of the fact that no bonus was paid to them at the time they undertook to farm in that way.
I was not objecting to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No, but I could understand if the hon. gentleman did object. I am sure, however, he will not object to this particular policy, as some other hon. members on the other side have done, since it is to carry out pretty much the principle which he was advocating last fall-and I think he made that fairly plain the other day when he was speaking in this house.
It was not to that matter in particular, however, that I wished to refer at the moment, but rather to the fact that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie made a statement in this debate on April 4 in which he said:
I was surprised when the Minister of Agriculture declared that he had embodied in this government proposal a large part of the recommendations made by the advisory committee of the wheat board and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Well, he may have adopted some of the minor suggestions but certainly none of the essentials.
Mr. LEADER.: That is absolutely true. That is a true statement.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is what my hon. friend stated. We will see about the other matter. On March 27 in this house I made a speech which included certain references to that particular policy, and some of those references were afterwards dealt with in the house by other speakers. On page 1922 will be found the report of what I said. Some time in January the Federation of Agriculture came to Ottawa and presented their resolutions, and the hon. member for Weyburn said it was January 27. I then proceeded to read the recommendations:
Wheat. In the days that lie ahead, it may be that a measure of adjustment of agricultural production may be found necessary in

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
the great wheat-growing areas of the prairie provinces, which may involve the re-appraisal of western agricultural resources so that a balance in agricultural production may be established.
Well, is not that in exact line with the proposal that is before the house at the present time, that something ought to be done in the days that are ahead of us in order to have a re-appraisal of the kind of agriculture which we have had, and to encourage something in another direction?
In the meantime, the problem created by heavy surpluses is a very real one for the western wheat grower.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture recommends:
Listen to the recommendations.
(1)	That while an adjustment programme may be found necessary in the future, it is not advisable at the present time to introduce compulsory restriction of acreage seeded to wheat.
We have not introduced compulsory reduction of acreage seeded to wheat. We have made a proposal exactly along the line suggested in the preamble to the resolution, that we should be preparing for the time ahead when some readjustment should be made, and we have given some inducement to farmers to change their method. But we have not said that they must change it.
But you are doing it indirectly.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Not indirectly. There is no compulsion about it. A farmer can say to-morrow when he seeds his wheat, "I will pay no attention whatever to these regulations; I will go ahead and sow wheat, believing that some day there will be a government in Canada that will let me market all the wheat I grow." He can say that and go ahead.
That is exactly what I am going to do.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
What we say with reference to the matter is this. We are not compelling the farmers of the west to reduce their acreage, but we are offering them some inducement to do so. The recommendations continue:
(2)	For the coming crop year, we believe that the dominion government, through the wheat board, should undertake to announce the total amount of wheat of which it is prepared to accept delivery.
We have announced that it is 230,000,000 bushels, but the hon. member for Portage la Prairie does not believe that that is essential to the carrying out of the policy. I would ask him, what is essential?
I have agreed to that.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, my hon. friend has agreed to it, but that does not mean that we do not accept any of the recommendations of the federation of agriculture.

On a question of privilege,
I did not state that the government accepted all of the recommendations or did not accept them or left some of them out. I said that the essential was left out, which is the increased price which all farmers and farm organizations, the wheat board and the pools as well as myself in a previous speech have advocated- an initial higher price to take care of the average farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have the floor. I did not interrupt the hon. member when he was speaking. Here are the words which the hon. gentleman used:
Well, he may have adopted some of the minor suggestions but certainly none of the essentials.
One of the essentials was the amount of wheat of which we were going to accept delivery. The recommendations go on:
We believe that the amount of wheat which may be delivered by the grower in the crop season of 1941-42 should be based on the estimated amount which the wheat board may be reasonably expected to market during the 1941-42 crop year, including both export and domestic sales.
We got an estimate of that amount from the wheat board, and we got it as the result of recommendations of the advisory committee of the wheat board, on which there are representatives of every organization of wheat growers, and the Canadian federation of agriculture.
Having established the maximum amount which may be delivered, we recommend that the individual grower's delivery quota should be based on a policy which will preserve to each farm unit an equitable share of such maximum amount in proportion to the past production of the crop district in which it is located.
That is exactly the policy announced the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, recommended by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, recommended by the wheat pools of all three western provinces, recommended by every organization that has discussed it, representative of the farmers that grow wheat; and that is an essential recommendation brought before this government.
We will come to another one. My hon. friend may consider others more essential, but we will come to them. I said the other day:
That is as near as one can get to a word description of what was read into the policy the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon).

It is a description exactly of the whole policy announced, with the exception of the price section of it. Now coming to the price section:
That because of the restricted deliveries and in order to maintain the income of the western farm home, steps should be taken to increase the initial payment for wheat delivered in the crop year of 1941.
The only suggestion made as to the extent to which it ought to be increased was the proposal that there should be a processing tax of not less than SO cents a bushel, which, added to the processing tax of last year, would make the tax about three times the amount it was last year.
A processing tax of 50 cents a bushel would bring, under these proposals, about $24,000,000. That $24,000,000 it was proposed should be spread over the 230,000,000 bushels, which would result in about eleven cents a bushel being added to the price. Then it was suggested by some of the organizations that probably a little more than that should be added. There are reasons why a processing tax should be put on and reasons why it should not. Ever since this war began, we have been advocating that we should obtain the costs of the war as largely as possible from excess profits tax or income tax on those who have large profits or incomes as a result of the war. But a processing tax on bread or flour or wheat is not a tax levied on that part of the population. Such a processing tax is levied on bread and wheat eaters. Wheat is the food of the great mass of the people of this and all western countries. It is the food of the labouring people, the food of the farmers themselves. The two groups in Canada who would pay the greater part of this processing tax would be the labouring men and the farmers.
They have a good increase in the price of their labour to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is probably true so far as part of the labouring classes are concerned, but I think my hon. friend will find that at least as much bread is consumed by the farmers of Canada to-day as is consumed by those who can be termed labourers. In other words, the processing tax would come, in large proportion, right out of the pockets of the farmers themselves.
Give them ten cents a bushel on the 230,000,000 and they will not kick.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is the net increase suggested. Let me recall that the processing tax, if put on, would provide $24,000,000 which it was suggested be added to the initial payment, and $7,000,000 of which is

already levied, and that that should be the price which the farmer should obtain this year-not an advance, but the price which the farmer should obtain. That has been the proposal throughout in many of the resolutions passed, that we should establish a new initial payment; that we should add on the processing tax, and that if we should not make that the price, then we should raise it a little higher and make that the price, and the suggestion has been made that that higher level ought to be 85 cents. This legislation gives the farmer the possibility of getting his 70 cents advance and also the possibility of having distribution among the farmers of western Canada of $36,000,000 instead of $24,000,000. In addition, it makes it possible for the farmers also to have participation to some extent in the price for which the wheat is sold. My hon. friends have been discussing past prophecies with regard to participation. Because of past experience in war time I am not going to make any prophecy at this time. Nevertheless the farmer knows the position; he has the possibility of dividing this $36,000,000, and a proper division of that sum will mean an added' return on his quota which everyone has agreed should stand. It will mean 86 cents a bushel to the farmers on the quota if they properly distribute it among themselves, as they can do under the provisions of these regulations. Hon. members can estimate as closely as I can what the participation may amount to.
Then we must take this into consideration, that if the farmer follows the practice of accepting a quota on 65 per cent of his acreage and growing his wheat on 40 per cent of his acreage, which he can easily do if it is a fair year, he will have the possibility of earning sufficient to put his wheat price up, on the quota that he is allowed to deliver, to approximately 89 cents, not at Fort William but at the point of delivery. I should like to suggest to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) that if the essence of the suggestion of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is not contained in the provisions of this policy, then it is not contained because this makes possible a higher return than the suggestions of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
It is all very well for my hon. friends to shake their heads, but all one has to do is to sit down with a pencil with the farmers in their constituencies and explain this policy to them, and the good hard-headed farmers of western Canada will tell them that this is really better than the suggestions that have been made by some hon. members.

Purely theoretical.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
(5)	It is anticipated that at the end of the current crop year, all existing^ grain storage facilities will be filled. We believe that these surpluses of bread grains may become an important factor in our war effort and that in the meantime they should be regarded as a reserve which will ensure a constant supply of wheat to Great Britain in the event of possible crop failure in the course of the war, and also be available to meet the needs of the people of Europe when the war is won.
That is a statement with which I think we will all agree, at least all who come from western Canada.
(6)	In view of the foregoing, and because we believe that the maintenance of reserve stocks of grain on the farm provides an effective form of crop insurance under existing conditions, we recommend that the dominion government be asked to provide financial assistance to farmers for the construction of adequate farm storage facilities to enable the farmer to adjust his deliveries in accordance with the system outlined above.
I understand that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and I disagree as to which proposed that kind of thing first. Nevertheless we both proposed it, so all I wish to say is that when I was placing this matter before the committee I stated that the time to make the final decision with regard to that part of the policy had not yet arrived; that if we have a good crop in western Canada this year, if on the acreage on which we are trying to grow
230,000,000 bushels we grow more than that- and I am scarcely correct in saying we are trying to grow 230,000,000 bushels; we are trying to grow 307,000,000 bushels, because it takes 77,000,000 bushels to take care of other demands apart from the consumption of wheat for flour-there may be a storage problem confronting the farmer and the government which may have to be given consideration, but other possibilities arise also.
Then No. 7:
It is recommended that the practice inaugurated during the present crop year, of paying farm storage, be continued through the coming crop season, and that the amount of the farm storage accruing due to individual farmers be used to repay any advances made to them which may be made for the purpose of providing additional storage facilities.
Who suggested that first?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not sure about that at the moment, but it does not make much difference; it was accepted by everyone.

With regard to the
statement about considering the matter of paying storage, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said this in No. 5 of his recommendations :
The Canadian wheat board will continue to pay storage to the producers on the same basis as 1940-41 but only on the undelivered portion of the 230,000,000 bushels.
It is very definite.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, the minister indicated to the committee a few minutes ago that the policy anticipates that the government will take delivery of only 230,000,000 bushels this year, and we are asking the farmers to try to cut the acreage down to the point that there will be only 230,000,000 bushels to be delivered for sale during this coming year. I anticipate that the farmers are going to try to do that, and they may be successful. If they are not, there may be some other problems confronting us at that time. But we must find out first whether the crop is 307,000,000 bushels or more or less.

Since it is anticipated that practically no elevator storage space will be available at the time of the 1941 harvest, we recommend that the dominion government authorize the Canadian wheat board to make cash advances against that portion of the 1941 crop which the farmer can deliver under the arrangement outlined above during the crop year 1941-42.
All I wish to say in that regard is that this policy was advocated a year ago. When the Minister of Mines and Resources and I met a committee in Winnipeg to discuss the question, and did not accept that proposal, we were condemned from one end of western Canada to the other. We suggested that there should not be an advance made on the farmer's wheat in August, but that this matter should be left for consideration later in the season. That was done. Then the Department of Trade and Commerce, acting under the powers given it in the legislation of last session, set up quotas which distributed the delivery of the wheat over the entire year. This year every farm organization in western Canada, including the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, asked the government to continue that policy. Therefore, just because farm and other organizations agitate against a policy does not mean that in the long run that policy will not turn out to be the right one. In spite of the fact that there was greater opposition to the policy of a year ago than so far there has been to this policy, the policy of last year now is accepted by every farm organization in Canada as having been the best policy in the interests of the farmer. It has been accepted not only

by farm organizations. The retail merchants' association, whose representative at the Winnipeg meeting a year ago condemned the policy, are satisfied with it to-day. Grain organizations are satisfied with it. Implement companies are satisfied with it. Farmers are satisfied with it. Banks are satisfied with it, though nearly all these people condemned it a year ago. So I would suggest that hon. members may now be condemning something that they will be supporting a year from now, and that it is not enough to say that because someone condemns a certain thing at a certain time, that thing is not right.
To deal further with the question raised by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, I would suggest that every single recommendation to which I have referred, which can be carried out, has been carried out with the exception of setting a higher price for the delivery of wheat in the initial stages. But I submit that this policy makes better provision, in the final disposition of the crop and the assistance it gives, than would the proposal which was placed before the government by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
They do not agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Well, ever since 1922 I have been receiving delegations from farm organizations almost annually, either as a member of a government, as leader of a government, as leader of an opposition or as a member of another government; and I have never seen the time when any government could accept all the recommendations placed before it by a farm organization or, so far as I know, any other organization. If on this occasion we have come so close to it as to miss out on only one recommendation, then I think we are about as close as any government ever came to accepting the resolutions of a farm organization. I believe that if we had accepted all their recommendations, they would have believed, after they left Ottawa, that their visit had been a failure; they would have thought they had missed out on something. Therefore, if we have not gone to the extent of giving them just what they asked for, in just the way they asked for it-
Or any other way.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
-I still do not think we have departed very far from what they requested. An hon. member says "Or any other way." I would ask one question. Why was it that farm organizations from all across Canada, meeting in Toronto, were not able to insert a price in their resolution?
IMr. Gardiner.]
Because they left it to the discretion of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Probably for the same reason that it would be difficult for any national organization to determine a price.
Does the minister really think the farmers will get 89 cents for this crop?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I really think some
farmers, who follow the principles of the resolutions now before the committee and put them into effect one hundred per cent, as they can be put into effect, will get 89 cents on their quota.
Would the minister say the majority?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not going to say the majority; I am not sufficiently acquainted with just what farmers will do under given circumstances.

Would the minister
explain how that will work out?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: A certain number of farmers will get that return; and it will vary from about 80 cents up, depending upon what they do if they take advantage of these provisions. I should, however, like to add that this return will be on only a limited amount of wheat. I do not want anyone to go away from this house with the idea that the farmer would be making money if he received 89 cents on that limited quantity, because he will cut his wheat down to 40 per cent of what he grew last year, and he will collect that price only on his restricted deliveries.
He will have a lower income.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Probably in the long run he will have a lower income. This house is attempting to give the farmer back something of what this war has taken away from him. We are not trying to give it all back; and my judgment is that the farmers of the west, and the farmers of all Canada, do not expect the government to give them back everything they may be losing as a result of the war. They do expect two or three things. They expect this government will see to it that others who are engaged in work having to do with the war do not get away with excess profits as a result of such war activity.
I think they expect this government to see that wages are not paid which will take all the labour away from the farms and place it in industry. They expect these things, and

Supply-Agriculture*-Wheat Acreages
they have a right to expect some action to be taken in these two directions. But assuming that proper action will be taken with regard to these two difficulties, either by the men themselves in connection with labour, or by industry itself in engaging labour, or by industry itself in relation to profits, or by the government insisting that industry and labour take these steps, then I think the farmer will tell you that he is prepared to sacrifice just as much as anyone else in Canada in the interests of the mother country and in the interests of Canada itself, in order to press this war to a successful conclusion.
With this in mind I would suggest to the committee that no good purpose will be served by holding up this estimate. Probably this matter will be discussed all over again when we return after the Easter adjournment. We shall have to go on with the policy laid down in the regulations which have been adopted under the War Measures Act. I would suggest that we go on with it and do the best we can to make it work. Then, after we have done all we can, if it does not work I am quite prepared to come back here after the recess, or next fall, or any other time, and listen to severe criticism from all sides of this house because of the fact that, under this proposal, the farmer did not receive what he should have received, having regard to the difficulties with which we are faced at the present time. If we do that, I think we can get on with the other work of the house. When we go back to our constituents in the west we can say, "The house has passed the estimate. They have not agreed on the whole principle; they are not all satisfied that it is the right thing for you, but this is the way you can put it into effect." Then, having given them that guidance, let us watch over it for a season. And if we want to criticize, let us criticize. There is always the possibility that a year from now we may be feeling just about the same with regard to this as we feel with regard to the quota system which was put into effect last year.
Mr. Chairman-
On a question of privilege. I claim the right to answer the Minister of Agriculture.
That is not a question of privilege.
Just a moment; on a question of privilege-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who is leading the house now has the floor. Is it the pleasure of the committee that lie should have the floor?
Yes.
No. I rise to a question of privilege. Surely, Mr. Chairman, a member lias some rights. On a question of privilege I ask permission to say a word or two in answer to the Minister of Agriculture.

I would say to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie that no one in the house, least of all myself, wishes to deny him the opportunity of making any reply he thinks necessary, or replying to anything in the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture to which he may take objection. But it was understood that the committee would rise and ask leave to sit again this day in order that before adjournment of the house at six o'clock the amendment moved some weeks ago by the hon. member for Haldimand on the motion to go into supply could be reestablished on the order paper. I am sure the hon. member for Portage la Prairie will believe me when I say no one wishes to deny him the right to reply.
Give me two minutes.
This other matter was agreed upon, and the government wishes to live up to the understanding. I therefore move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again this day.
On a question of privilege, I take the stand that I am being denied the right to speak.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Let the hon. member speak a few minutes, then.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The motion is not
debatable.
If my hon. friend will finish what he has to say in a few minutes, so that we can handle the other business before six o'clock, it will be all right.
It will not take long.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The motion will stand, then.

I wish to say that I feel highly complimented in that the Minister of Agriculture should brood over and consider the speech I made in the house recently. Evidently it is the truth that hurts. I take this position in the committee to-day, namely, that in my speech I uttered nothing but the truth when I pointed out that the policy of the Minister of Agriculture does not embody the essentials. The first essential, as I take it, was that the people of Canada- and I will limit this to western Canada-should

have a higher initial price. Another essential was connected with the processing tax. Never did the Minister of Agriculture or any other hon. member hear me defend the processing tax on the floor of the house. That was one of the essentials, I am willing to admit; but the essential thing is the increase in the initial price. They do ask for that. But what does the government do? The farmers have asked for bread and the government gives them a stone. I will defy the Minister of Agriculture to come out into my constituency, and I will resign to-morrow and I will fight this argument in that constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have been in your constituency before.

We are always glad to see you. I offer that invitation, to come out and settle it before the highest tribunal in the land.
I should like to put on Hansard what the minister did say:
I think that with the exception of the definite suggestion that a processing tax be levied and that the initial payment be increased-with nothing definite as to the amount-and with the possible exception of the proposal made in one other section of these recommendations, we have already embodied in the policy which is before the house the greater part of what has been asked for in the resolutions of both bodies.
I say the essential thing is the initial payment.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My hon. friend has said he was surprised to hear me say that.

I did not interrupt the
minister. They have given us what I claim, and what I believe the people of western Canada will claim is a fool policy, and not what the people of western Canada have asked for.

As a matter of
privilege I should be allowed to answer the minister's reference to me.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I shall have to have an opportunity to reply.
I have moved that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again this day.
Shall we come back later to the committee stage?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The motion is "to sit again this day". Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the motion?
Mr. ROSS ISouris): Then, as a matter of privilege, I am not allowed to make a statement in reply?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The hon. member made a forty-minute speech.
I still have twenty minutes coming to me.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have not had an opportunity to distribute copies of the regulations. I shall leave them at the end of the table, and anyone who wishes to have one may take it. They are not exactly word-perfect, because I believe there are one or two points at which typographical errors may be found.
Progress reported.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at this stage I wish to move an amendment-

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have the floor on this motion.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, the minister has not the floor. This is a new motion.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us have a little fair play.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have risen to move an amendment based on the condition of agriculture. I think it will be agreed by all hon. members that in time of war the morale of this nation cannot be as it should be if agriculture is pauperized. Agriculture taken as a whole in Canada is in a lamentable condition, and it is an anomalous condition of affairs that Canada, a great producer of food, should, in a world which sooner or later will require foodstuffs, try to find means to bring about a reduction in the production of wheat.
I move therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Peel:
That all the words after "that" in the motion be struck out, and that the following be substituted therefor:
it be resolved that the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in order that it may receive a just and fair return, and thus be enabled to make that contribution to Canada's war effort which is so desirable, and which our agricultural population so greatly desire to make.
On motion of Mr. Diefenbaker the debate was adjourned.

Mr. CRERAR moved the adjournment of the house.
Are we to understand that we cannot now discuss the resolution which was before the committee of supply until the motion of the hon. member for Lake Centre is disposed of?

I will say to my hon. friend that it was our intention at this point to move the adjournment of the house, and not to sit to-night. This matter can be taken up again at some future time, when the house reassembles. We have had a pretty lengthy discussion; the committee has been patient, and I am sure that most of the members will welcome as I do adjourning at six o'clock.
I trust that when we reassemble on the 28th of this month we shall all come back refreshed and reinvigorated for the work that lies ahead.

Do I understand that
we are now adjourning until the 28th of April?
Yes.

That is a violation of
the understanding reached between us the other evening. It was agreed that the regulations would be discussed, and that if we agreed to forego a meeting of the house on Wednesday we would adjourn at eleven o'clock to-night. This is the first I have heard of any different arrangement, and I think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is right, that before we go back to the west we should know what the regulations mean.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: May I say this, to carry out an undertaking I gave to members from the west in the far corner of the house and in other parts. It was impossible for us to carry out the undertaking in connection with sitting to-night on account of the misunderstanding that apparently arose over the arrangement of yesterday, and the official opposition being desirous of going back to a discussion of the want of confidence motion to-day, which took us out of the other discussion. I am prepared to-night to meet in any room that may be named, any or all of the members from the west or from the east to discuss the regulations and go into them fully. I suppose the railway committee room will be available, and there or in any other room that is convenient I shall be glad to go into details of the regulations and to answer any questions that hon. members may wish to ask about them.

Why not
carry on here as agreed?

Motion agreed to, on division, and the house adjourned at 6.05 p.m. until Monday, April 28.
